title: Participate in business continuity planning and exercises
summary: Business continuity keeps prioritized business functions operating through disruption by aligning people, processes, technology, facilities, suppliers, communications, and recovery priorities.
outcome: Given a business disruption, identify critical functions and dependencies, select continuity workarounds or recovery priorities, exercise the plan, and capture improvements that protect the mission rather than only the technology.
managerMindset: Continuity starts with the mission and its tolerable interruption, then works backward to people, process, technology, facilities, suppliers, and communications.

sections.title: Plan continuity around functions and dependencies
sections.body: Business continuity planning identifies critical functions, impacts, priorities, tolerances, resources, dependencies, and acceptable workarounds. A business impact analysis helps owners describe consequences over time, while security and technology teams translate those needs into service, data, identity, facility, supplier, and recovery requirements. Choose priority and recovery assumptions with the business owner; do not derive them from a technology inventory alone. Continuity is broader than disaster recovery because it includes manual operations, staffing, alternate communications, customers, and external dependencies.
keyPoints: Business owners define mission priority and impact; technical teams help make the requirement executable.
Dependencies include people, suppliers, data, facilities, identity, communications, and regulatory obligations.
A workaround can preserve a function while a technical recovery proceeds, but it needs authorization, safety, data, and evidence controls.

sections.title: Exercise continuity, communicate, and improve
sections.body: Continuity exercises test decisions, communications, roles, workarounds, supplier coordination, and transition criteria. Define scope, objective, observers, evidence, communications, and stop criteria; use injects that reflect missing people, limited facilities, delayed vendors, degraded data, or public communication pressure. Record what participants assumed, what worked, what failed, and which owner will change the plan, contract, training, technology, or priority. A corrective action is complete only when the changed continuity capability is accepted and retested.
keyPoints: A continuity exercise should test business decisions and dependencies, not only system failover.
Exercise communications should distinguish a test from a real event and protect sensitive plans.
Corrective actions should be prioritized, owned, evidenced, and retested.

workedExamples.title: Supplier outage during a customer deadline
workedExamples.situation: A critical outsourced transaction service becomes unavailable while the internal application and data remain healthy.
workedExamples.reasoning: Activate continuity procedures, confirm business priority and customer commitments, use an approved manual or alternate provider workaround, communicate accurately, protect data and approvals, and track the supplier dependency. The exercise should test contract contacts, identity, data exchange, staffing, and return criteria.

distinctions.difference: BC maintains prioritized business functions through disruption; DR restores technology and supporting capabilities as one part of continuity.
A BIA describes business impact and priority over time; risk assessment evaluates threats, likelihood, and impact to guide treatment.

misconceptions.misconception: Continuity is the IT department's recovery plan.
misconceptions.correction: Business owners, people, facilities, suppliers, communications, security, and technology all contribute to continuity.

misconceptions.misconception: A documented alternate site proves continuity.
misconceptions.correction: People, data, identity, suppliers, communications, workarounds, and acceptance must be exercised as well.

recallChecks.prompt: What does a BIA contribute to continuity planning?
recallChecks.answer: It describes critical functions, consequences and tolerances over time, priorities, resources, and dependencies.

recallChecks.prompt: Why include manual workarounds in an exercise?
recallChecks.answer: A function may need to continue before technical recovery is available, so people and process can be the temporary control.

recallChecks.prompt: What should an exercise produce beyond attendance?
recallChecks.answer: Observed decisions, assumptions, failures, evidence, assigned improvements, owners, due dates, and retest conditions.

recallChecks.prompt: What belongs in a continuity exercise scope?
recallChecks.answer: The function, dependencies, people, time window, assumptions, injects, communications, safety boundaries, evidence, and success criteria.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: A payroll service is down and the continuity plan says 'contact the vendor' but names no alternate process or decision owner.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Escalate the continuity gap, identify business priority and tolerable delay, define a controlled workaround, and update and exercise the plan.
scenarioSeeds.why: A contact list is not a continuity capability by itself.

studyPlan.learn: Study critical functions, BIA, dependencies, priorities, workarounds, continuity exercises, communications, and corrective actions.
studyPlan.connect: Connect D7.13 to D1 continuity, D7.10 recovery, D7.11 DR, and D2 data and supplier dependencies.
studyPlan.apply: Run a continuity scenario for a critical function whose supplier and staff are unavailable.
studyPlan.revisit: Explain which business owner decision would set the priority before technical recovery begins.

review.notes: Independent AI review only. Claim evidence, exact content fingerprints, scope checks, visual and memory-map assessments are recorded in knowledge/quality/. No human expert review or exam-readiness claim.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: How do business owners turn disruption consequences into continuity priorities, workable alternatives, and evidence from an exercise?
visualLearningContract.misconception: Business continuity is simply IT disaster recovery, or a system inventory can set recovery priority.
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: Critical function, BIA, priority, manual workaround, external dependency, communications, and remediation.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not assign a universal RTO, exercise frequency, or claim a particular supplier SLA.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: The payment platform is intact but the call center and verification vendor are unavailable. Which function, workaround, dependency, and evidence must the exercise test?
visualLearningContract.textFallback:
business continuity: The organization’s ability and planning discipline to sustain prioritized business functions through disruption and transition to normal operations.. Decision: Frame continuity around essential outcomes, people, facilities, suppliers, data, and communications—not only IT recovery.. Failure/example: Restoring servers while customer support and approvals cannot operate is not business continuity.
continuity planning: The owner-led process of identifying disruption scenarios, priorities, resources, alternatives, roles, and recovery/return criteria.. Decision: Plan with business, facilities, HR, suppliers, and technology owners before an event; revise when their assumptions change.. Failure/example: A technology-only plan may omit staff shortages or contractual dependencies that halt the function.
critical function: A business activity whose unacceptable interruption drives a continuity priority, such as payments, safety response, or regulatory reporting.. Decision: Have the business owner identify the function and consequence; do not infer criticality from system cost or popularity.. Failure/example: Treating a high-cost but deferrable system as first priority can delay a time-sensitive obligation.
business impact analysis: A structured assessment of disruption consequences over time that supplies business requirements for continuity and recovery.. Decision: Use business-owner input to determine impacts, tolerances, dependencies, and priority; validate when business conditions change.. Failure/example: An asset inventory cannot reveal the mounting legal or safety consequence of a delayed business process.
continuity priority: The agreed order in which business functions receive continuity resources based on time-sensitive impact and accepted tolerances.. Decision: Set priority through accountable business decisions informed by BIA, then communicate the tradeoff to resource owners.. Failure/example: Letting the loudest technical owner choose priority can starve a more time-critical function.
manual workaround: A predesigned nonstandard way to perform a critical function when normal people, place, process, or technology is unavailable.. Decision: Use when it can safely sustain the function for a defined period; test staffing, records, approvals, and later reconciliation.. Failure/example: Paper orders without later reconciliation can preserve availability while corrupting records.
continuity exercise: A planned practice of continuity roles, alternatives, and decisions under a disruption scenario.. Decision: Choose an exercise that tests the business function and its dependencies, not merely technical failover.. Failure/example: A server-failover test that never involves business staff leaves continuity of the customer process unknown.
exercise scope: The stated functions, locations, participants, dependencies, scenario, boundaries, and evidence included in a continuity exercise.. Decision: Include the business function’s real dependencies and explicit exclusions so evidence can be interpreted honestly.. Failure/example: Excluding the verification vendor from a payment continuity exercise produces a misleading pass.
continuity evidence: Objective records showing whether the prioritized function, communication, alternative process, and acceptance conditions performed as planned.. Decision: Collect outcomes such as timelines, work products, decision records, reconciliation, and owner acceptance against stated criteria.. Failure/example: Attendance and enthusiastic discussion do not prove the function continued within its tolerance.
